Where do insertions come from? Are the origins of insertions in the vicinity (1D or 3D) of the
rearranged regions?
Insertions are rearrangements with one or several donor sequences inserted into a non-adjacent
chromosomal locus. Donor sequences originate from experimentally induced as well as spontaneous
genome instability11. While variant analysis allows us to infer the insertion site within the reference
genome, it remains challenging to pinpoint the exact donor locus of the inserted sequence or to
establish whether the insertion originated in the spatial vicinity of the rearranged region.
Major comments 2: The authors should also discuss that error free/prone repair mechanisms might
differ between irradiations sources in addition to the number of DSB induced. The balance between
these parameters lead to the outcome of repair that is measured by the number of SV. In other words,
the repair pathways used by S. lividans upon irradiation might differ and lead to different outcome
that either correlates or not with the DSB formation.
As you mentioned, mutational outcome depends not only on the number of DSBs but also on
the nature of the DNA damage and the subsequent cellular repair response across different
irradiation sources. According to your comment, we have expanded our Discussion section (now
lines 308-322) to incorporate this context, with the specific additions as follows:
To cope with irradiation-induced DNA DSBs, cells kickstart the error-prone NHEJ pathway
for rapid repair. This survival mechanism directly contributes to the generation of SVs. The
mutational outcome depends not only on the number of DSBs but also on the nature of the DNA
damage and the subsequent cellular repair response across different irradiation sources14. For
instance, high LET radiation, such as HEPE, produce complex and clustered DNA lesions almost
instantaneously that are challenging to repair and might be preferentially handled by rapid but error-
prone mechanisms like NHEJ15. In contrast, UV radiation mainly generates cyclobutane–pyrimidine
dimers, which are commonly repaired by photolyase-mediated photoreactivation47. Plasma
irradiation, however, induces oxidative DNA damage or strand breaks through reactive species
intracellularly48. Such oxidative DNA lesions are mainly repaired by two mechanisms: base excision
repair (BER) and nucleotide excision repair (NER)49. SSBs are typically repaired by BER, whereas
DSBs are generally repaired by homologous recombination (HR) or NHEJ mechanisms. Differences
in the nature of DNA damage and repair mechanisms explain why HEPE generates more SVs. A
more thorough understanding of the mechanisms underlying SVs formation will be advanced
through continued characterization of SVs breakpoints and the development in vitro and in vivo
model systems that can generate chromosomal SVs
Major comments 3: I would suggest to show the Hi-C results as matrix to better highlight the
putative change in 3D organization upon irradiation and repair. This would allow to show multi
contacts.
Thanks for your advice.
We have now included genome-wide Hi-C contact matrices comparing the control and
irradiated conditions in the revised manuscript to illustrate global changes in 3D architecture. These
new matrix plots has been added as Figure S3 in the revised manuscript. The description in the
Results section (lines 166-176) has been updated to correspond with these additions, as shown below:
To investigate potential alterations in 3D conformation in HEPE mutant, we compared the
chromosome architecture of the wild type (WT) and the mutant strain (H_D1) using high-throughput
chromosome conformation capture (Hi-C). First, circus plot (Fig. 3c) of the significant interactions
(see Materials and Methods) revealed a substantial increase in interaction number in mutant (8830)
compared to WT (458). Furthermore, the 3D architecture (Fig. 3d) showed that WT maintain a
compact chromosome organization, whereas the mutant exhibited a more relaxed conformation.
This difference can be elucidated by the differential interaction and compact analysis (see Materials
and Methods). As shown in the differential interaction heatmap and the compact matrix (Fig. S3),
WT is enriched in long-range interactions, maintaining its tighter spatial connectivity. In contrast,
mutant showed enhanced short-range interactions, corresponding to a looser spatial organization.
Figure S3. Interaction difference analysis between WT S. lividans 1326 and its mutant (H_D1)
derived from HEPE mutagenesis. a, The differential interaction heatmap (mutant versus WT). Both
axed represent genomic positions in bins. Red or blue indicates loci with stronger interaction
intensity in the mutant or WT sample, respectively. Deeper color denotes a greater difference. b,
Genome compaction changes between samples. The interaction strength differences at various
genomic distances (y-axis) for each locus (x-axis) are compared. Red or blue indicates stronger
interactions in WT or mutant, respectively. Deeper color denotes a greater difference.
Minor points 1: Figure legends should be more detailed
Thanks for your suggestion, we have changed all figure legends with adding sufficient details,
you can find these newly added details in blue color within file Article File with tracked changes.
Minor points 2: The duration of the UV irradiation is not a dose but depends on the dose rate. Thus,
UV doses must be given in J/cm2 or J/m2.
The light energy is calculated as the product of light intensity and irradiation time. Using an
ultraviolet lamp with a light intensity of 48 μW/cm², the resulting light energies at irradiation times
of 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180, and 210 seconds are calculated to be 1.44, 2.88, 4.32, 5.76, 7.20, 8.64,
and 10.08 mJ/cm², respectively. This description has been added to the main text lines 451-453.
Minor points 3: The TUNEL assays have been performed immediately after irradiation. I am
wondering whether some irradiation sources would induce breaks with different kinetics. This
should be discussed or reference should be added
Thanks for your advice.
TUNEL assay detects DNA strand breaks by using terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase to
catalyze the attachment of modified deoxynucleotides to the DNA broken ends. In our study, the
TUNEL assay was performed immediately after irradiation primarily to capture the direct DNA
strand breaks induced by the radiation source used. Our main goal was to compare the initial DNA
damage response across the treatment groups, prior to the initiation of any repair processes.
However, your concern regarding the induction of DNA breaks with different kinetics by some
irradiation sources is justified. This variation arises from differences in the complexity of the
resulting DNA lesions and the repair pathways involved. Different types of damage engage distinct
cellular repair pathways and operate at varying repair rates. This may affect the intensity of the
"break signals" detected by TUNEL at a specific time point. As you suggested, we have now
expanded the Discussion section (now lines 308-322) to address the potential influence of radiation
sources on repair pathways. The relevant text corresponds to the response to Major Comment 2
above. We have also added supporting references (15, 46-48).
Reviewer 2:
Major Comments 1: HEPE-induced structural variations (SVs) drive the activation of cryptic
biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs), leading to increased secondary metabolite production. However,
the mechanistic link between specific SVs and BGC activation is not fully established, the causality
between specific SVs and metabolite production could be explored more mechanistically, e.g.,
RNA-seq data (or qRT-PCR validation) to demonstrate that specific BGCs (e.g., gbn, fdn) are
transcriptionally upregulated in HEPE mutants, or discuss correlations of specific SV types (e.g.,
translocations, deletions) with changes in the regulatory architecture of BGCs.
Thanks for your advice.
Based on your suggestion, we have performed additional RNA-seq experiments. We selected
the S. lividans 1326 wild-type strain and three HEPE mutants in which the act or red gene clusters
were activated for transcriptome sequencing. The results demonstrate that transcription levels of
numerous secondary metabolic genes were upregulated in HEPE mutants, including those
responsible for ACT and RED biosynthesis (new results are presented in Figure S4). These mutant
strains harbored various types of SVs, such as insertions, deletions, and translocations, with no
common SV identified across all mutants. The results indicate an inconsistent association between
the SVs in different mutant strains and the activation of the target gene clusters. This is further
supported by the observation that in the three mutant strains, the specific genes that were upregulated
within the ACT and RED gene clusters also varied. Consequently, the mechanisms underlying
cluster activation likely vary among strains, which led us to forgo the idea of employing the
challenging approach by performing individual gene knockouts to validate the impact of different
SV variants on metabolic activation.
In addition, transcriptomic data revealed extensive metabolic alterations in the mutants, which
were further reflected in the 3D genome conformation. We supplemented the analysis by comparing
the 3D genomic architecture of mutant strain with that of the wild-type (WT) to elucidate the local
or global genome changes. First, circus plot (New Fig. 3c) of the significant interactions revealed a
substantial increase in interaction number in mutant (8830) compared to WT (458). Specifically, the
interaction intensity within the ACT and RED gene cluster regions was markedly enhanced,
indicating significant alterations in spatial architecture. Furthermore, the 3D architecture (Fig. 3d) showed that WT maintain a compact chromosome organization, whereas the mutant exhibited a
more relaxed conformation. This structural relaxation likely facilitates the binding of RNA
polymerase and other transcriptional machinery to DNA by increasing physical accessibility to
regulatory regions and gene promoters, ultimately modulating the expression of secondary
metabolite BGC32. This global architecture change is unlikely to be caused by small-scale SNVs or
indels, but is primarily attributed to large-scale SVs.
In summary, while a direct causative link between a specific SV and transcriptional
upregulation remains unconfirmed, the collective evidence supports a central role for SVs in driving
the broad transcriptomic reprogramming, metabolic remodeling, and altered 3D genome
architecture observed in these mutants.
Figure S4. Volcano plot of differentially expressed genes between WT S. lividans 1326 and its
mutants derived from HEPE mutagenesis. H_D1, H_D28, and H_D34 were three mutants obtained
by HEPE irradiation. Each point represents a gene. The x-axis shows the log (fold change) in

Major Comments 2: The Hi-C analysis reveals changes in chromatin architecture, but the link
between SV-induced 3D genome remodeling and metabolite activation remains speculative. Can it
be identified whether any SVs disrupt known regulatory domains, such as promoters, repressors, or
insulation boundaries?
Thanks for your advice.
We analyzed genomic variations in mutant strains of S. lividans 1326 with activated
actinorhodin (ACT) and undecylprodigiosin (RED) gene clusters but did not identify any SVs that
directly broke the pathway-specific regulatory proteins within the clusters. However, in several
HEPE mutants, we detected SVs—including deletions and translocations—in the upstream regions
of genes encoding TetR or SARP family regulators. The genes redD and actII-4 encode positive
regulators for the biosynthesis of RED and ACT, respectively. The regulatory factors encoded by
both genes belong to the SARP family. Another ACT pathway-specific regulator exists in S. lividans:
ActII-1, a member of the TetR family. It has been reported to act as a repressor of ACT biosynthesis
(See additional document). These variants near regulatory genes may influence their expression or
function, thereby potentially driving the activation of the ACT or RED clusters.
Structural variations (SVs), encompassing insertions, deletions, translocations, and other
rearrangements, exert their impact not only through disrupting discrete genetic elements like
promoters or repressors but, more profoundly, by remodeling the 3D genome architecture and
rewiring metabolic networks. To test this, we conducted two critical experiments: transcriptome
sequencing (RNA-seq) and comparative 3D genome conformation analysis between S.
lividans 1326 WT and mutant strains. As detailed in our response to your Major Comment 1 above,
transcriptomic analysis revealed that in three distinct mutant strains, the upregulated biosynthetic
genes responsible for ACT and RED production varied significantly, indicating notable differences
in their respective activation mechanism. The mutants displayed extensive transcriptional
reprogramming and a globally altered chromosome architecture. We believe that SVs disrupt both
the linear DNA sequence and the higher-order 3D conformation, thereby driving the observed
enhancement in metabolite production. In future work, we will perform more in-depth studies to
provide more experimental evidence linking these SVs to metabolite activation.
Major Comments 3: The comparison of six irradiation technologies lacks normalization for
absorbed radiation dose. For a fair comparison, please provide quantitative values such as dose
equivalents (Gy or kGy), D10 values, and LET for each treatment.
We sincerely appreciate your comment regarding the necessity of dose normalization for fair
comparison of different irradiation technologies. While we recognize the importance of normalized
dose metrics for direct comparison, the nature of six irradiation technologies presents challenges in
obtaining complete dose equivalence data. Specifically, UV employs photons, microwaves utilize
electromagnetic waves, X-ray and γ-ray are high-energy electromagnetic radiation, ARTP are based
on plasma, and HEPE involves electron beams. The fundamental differences in irradiation
mechanisms and energy level among these various types of irradiations makes it difficult to
standardize their doses uniformly. To address this limitation, we irradiated samples with four
incrementally increasing doses, covering the commonly used range from the lower to the upper
detection limits of the irradiation instrument.
Major Comments 4: The broad claim that HEPE is a “universal” tool for microbial strain
improvement is premature given that only five species were tested. Please either qualify this claim
or include additional examples from more phylogenetically diverse microbes.
We agree that describing HEPE as “universal” based on results from only five microbial strains
is premature. In this study, HEPE was applied to five strains spanning three phylogenetically distinct
groups: Escherichia coli (bacterium), Streptomyces griseobrunneus, Streptomyces fradiae,
and Streptomyces clavuligerus (actinomycetes), and Monascus purpureus (filamentous fungus).
While these representatives suggest broad applicability, we acknowledge that a more comprehensive
phylogenetic diversity would be required to support a claim of universality. Accordingly, we have
replaced the term “universal” with more accurate descriptors such as “broadly applicable” in the
main text.
Major Comments 5: The structural characterization of griseobrucins and fradibactins is impressive,
but the biological activity data are minimal. It would be better to test or discuss additional
bioactivities beyond basic antimicrobial screening.
Thank you for the positive assessment of our structural characterization work and for this
suggestion regarding the biological evaluation. In our initial biological screening, compounds
griseobrucins and fradibactins showed no antimicrobial activity against any of the tested bacterial
strains in vitro. According to your comment, we have conducted additional cytotoxic activity
screening using the CCK-8 assay. The compounds were evaluated against a panel of twenty human
cancer cell lines, including A549, MKN-45, HCT 116, HeLa, HepG2, K-562, 786-O, TE-1, 5637,
GBC-SD, L-02, MCF7, SF126, DU145, CAL-62, PATU8988T, HOS, A-375, A-673, 293T.
Regrettably, neither griseobrucins nor fradibactins demonstrated no discernible cytotoxic activity
against the tested human cancer cell lines.
The griseobrucins belong to the diketopiperazine (DKP) class of natural products. In addition
to their documented antibacterial and antitumor activities, recent researches have revealed that
DKPs compounds can participate in intercellular communication through quorum sensing49, exhibit
hypoglycemic effects50, and demonstrate antioxidant activity51. Inspired by these findings, we
propose that future research should include a systematic biological evaluation of the griseobrucins
to explore their potential pharmacological roles in quorum sensing regulation, oxidative stress
mitigation, and metabolic regulation. Additionally, fradibactin represent a carboxylic acid-
hydroxamic acid hybrid siderophore. Recent advances have shown that conjugating siderophore
molecules with antibiotics to utilize bacterial iron uptake systems for intracellular drug delivery
constitutes a promising strategy for developing novel antimicrobial agents52. Subsequent studies
could attempt to conjugate fradibactin with clinically relevant antibiotics and evaluate the
antimicrobial activity of the resulting conjugates against ESKAPE pathogens and other clinically
significant strains. The results and discussion regarding the bioactivity of these compounds have
been integrated into the main text (lines 328–333).
Major Comments 6: The HEPE-HiTMS approach is powerful, but no integration is shown between
the metabolomic and genomic datasets. Please clarify whether mutants producing new metabolites
shared common SVs or genomic rearrangements near the associated BGCs.
Our approach focused on validating the HEPE methodology using S. lividans 1326, where the
BGCs for ACT and RED are normally silent. The successful activation of these clusters confirmed
HEPE as an effective mutagen for cryptic BGCs. We sequenced 32 HEPE-induced S.
lividans mutants and observed a high frequency of SVs.
Building on this, the HEPE-HiTMS pipeline was employed and successfully identified two
novel classes of natural products. However, due to constraints in time and resources, we were unable
to conduct large-scale genome sequencing of the numerous mutant strains producing these new
metabolites. The high-throughput genome sequencing of S. lividans 1326 mutants provided
sufficient clues to connect SVs with metabolites production. Analysis of the existing sequencing
data from the ACT/RED-activating mutants in S. lividans 1326 revealed no shared, identical SVs or
genomic rearrangements in the vicinity of their respective BGCs. This finding is consistent with the
nature of HEPE as a non-targeted mutagen—the DNA damage it induces and the subsequent repair
processes are stochastic, leading to diverse genomic alterations even when the phenotypic outcome
(e.g., activation of a specific BGC) is similar. Furthermore, although no common SVs were observed
within the gene clusters themselves, the newly added transcriptomic and 3D conformational data
from the mutant strains-as detailed in our response to your Comment 1-reveal that both the ACT
and RED gene clusters are located within regions of significantly enhanced chromosome
interactions. This supports your hypothesis that SVs likely contribute to metabolite activation by
altering the spatial architecture surrounding the relevant BGCs.
Major Comments 7: The manuscript does not sufficiently compare HEPE to modern genome
engineering tools like CRISPR/Cas9 or BGC refactoring. Please discuss the advantages and
limitations of HEPE relative to synthetic biology approaches, especially in precision, scalability,
and strain traceability.
While synthetic biology approaches such as CRISPR/Cas9 enable targeted genomic edits, they
heavily rely on genetic engineering manipulation. In contrast, HEPE operates without the need for
genetic manipulation or the introduction of exogenous systems. This key advantage makes HEPE
particularly suitable for applications subject to strict regulatory constraints and for use in wild-type
industrial strains with limited genetic tools. Furthermore, as requested, we have now added a new
paragraph (now lines 334-350) to the Discussion section in the revised manuscript discussing the
advantages and limitations of HEPE compared to CRISPR/Cas9 or BGC refactoring approaches,
with particular emphasis on precision, scalability, and strain traceability. The detailed contents are
as follows:
While HEPE requires specialized accelerators, its mutagenic efficiency significantly reduces
screening time, workload and costs, offsetting initial investments. Compared to synthetic biology
approaches such as CRISPR/Cas9 or BGC refactoring, HEPE offers distinct advantages as well as
certain limitations. CRISPR/Cas9 enable targeted genomic edits but heavily relies on genetic
engineering manipulation. In contrast, HEPE operates without the need for genetic manipulation or
the introduction of exogenous systems, making it particularly suitable for applications subject to
strict regulatory constraints and for use in wild-type industrial strains with limited genetic tools. In
terms of precision, HEPE introduces random mutations across the genome, differing fundamentally
from the single-nucleotide accuracy of CRISPR/Cas9. Although this limits its utility for specific
edits, it allows for broad mutagenesis and discovery of unexpected functional mutations-thereby
serving as a valuable complement to targeted approaches. Regarding scalability, HEPE is highly
scalable for generating diverse mutant libraries in a single step, bypassing the need for complex
DNA construct design and transformation procedures required for CRISPR-based methos or BGC
refactoring. This makes it particularly efficient for high-throughput mutagenesis in non-model or
genetically recalcitrant strains. For strain traceability, CRISPR/Cas9 leaves precise and trackable
edits, whereas HEPE-induced mutations are stochastic and require whole-genome sequencing to
establish mutational profiles and track strain.
Major Comments 8: No discussion is included on the possible unintended effects of random SVs,
such as growth defects, metabolic imbalance, or genome instability. Please add phenotypic data,
e.g., growth curves, morphology, or biomass yield to assess off-target consequences of HEPE
mutagenesis.
Assessing the potential unintended effects of random SVs is necessary for evaluating the HEPE
mutagenesis method. We have now performed phenotype and growth curves analysis for randomly
selected HEPE-mutagenized clones alongside with the wild-type. As shown in the new Figure S5,
mutagenized clones exhibit reduced sporulation and delayed growth compared to the wild-type
strain. We have incorporated these results in the main text (lines 183-188) as follows:
Additionally, random SVs can have possible unintended effects, such as growth defects. To
assess off-target consequences of HEPE mutagenesis, three mutants were selected for phenotype
and growth curve analysis. Compared to WT strain, mutants exhibited reduced sporulation and
delayed growth (Fig. S5). Transcriptome data linked this phenotype to a marked downregulation of
the sporulation-associated gene sapA and the regulatory factors whiB and whiD, which control cell
division and spore septum formation33, 34 (Table S5).

H_D34 were three mutants obtained by HEPE irradiation. a, Mutants phenotypes of wild type (WT)
and selected mutant strains on solid media. b, Growth curve of WT and selected mutant strains in liquid
culture. Data are presented as mean ± SEM of two replicates cultures.
Table S5. Expression of sporulation-associated genes from RNA sequencing. H_D1, H_D28, and
H_D34 were three mutants obtained by HEPE irradiation. Compared to WT, all three mutant
strains exhibited a significant downregulation of gene expression (p < 0.001 in each case). Each
sample was performed with three replicates.

Major Comments 9: The functional validation of the fdn and gbn clusters (e.g., via gene knockouts
or overexpression) is minimal. It would strengthen the argument if you could show that disrupting
these clusters abolishes metabolite production in HEPE mutants.
We have knocked out the fdn gene cluster, which is responsible for fradibactins biosynthesis,
via the homologous recombination method. Mass spectra analysis confirmed the absence of signals
corresponding to the associated metabolites (Figure S11). We also knocked out the proposed gbn
gene cluster, putatively involved in griseobrucins biosynthesis, using the same method. However,
mass spectra analysis indicated that the related metabolites signals remained present, suggesting
that the proposed gbn cluster is not responsible for the biosynthesis of these compounds.
Considering identifying BGCs are not our main task of this study, we now removed the information
of previous predicted gbn BGC from our manuscript and started to discover the actual gene cluster
for griseobrucins in future work.
Figure S11. Gene inactivation of fdnA using the homologous recombination method. a, scheme of
the construction of fdnA replacement mutant. b, PCR confirmation of the fdnA inactivation by
insertion of an apramycin resistance-oriT cassette (aac(3)IV+oriT). d, verification of metabolite
alteration in fdnA inactivation mutant.
Minor Comments 1: The term “expression of metabolome profile” (Abstract, line 38-39) is
ambiguous. Consider rephrasing as “activation of secondary metabolite production” or
“enhancement of metabolite biosynthesis.”
We have followed your suggestion and replaced it with " activation of secondary metabolite
production ".
Minor Comments 2: Please avoid overuse of vague qualifiers such as “significantly” or “markedly”
unless supported by statistical metrics.
We have replaced these terms with more precise, quantitative descriptions or have provided
the corresponding statistical evidence where applicable.
Minor Comments 3: Please clarify how radiation doses for HEPE were selected and calibrated
relative to the other platforms.
Radiation doses for HEPE were 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8KGy. The minimum dose of 0.5
KGy was selected based on the lower limit of the instrument. To determine the optimal HEPE dose
for activating secondary metabolite production in the selected bacterial strain, a gradient of doses
was tested. The highest dose of 8 kGy was chosen based on preliminary experiments, which resulted
in a 99.7% lethality rate, representing a near-lethal condition.
While we recognize the importance of dose normalization, the irradiation source type of HEPE
is completely different from that of other platforms, and its energy is several orders of magnitude
higher. As such, direct dose normalization is not feasible. The irradiation source characteristics of
each platform have already been described in our response to your Major Comment 3. Consequently,
we established dose gradients for comparative analysis based on the operational range (from
minimum to maximum. Additionally, in the mutagenic efficiency section of this article, we
compared positive mutation frequency of each platform under conditions of comparable lethality.
This approach, to some extent, ensures a relatively equivalent basis for comparison.
Minor Comments 4: Several phrases are awkward or non-standard (e.g., “super pure helium,”
“expression of pigments stably expressed mutants,” “mutational stability”). Please revise for clarity
and consistent scientific terminology.
Thanks for your advice.
We have replaced “super pure helium”, “expression of pigments stably expressed mutants” and
“mutational stability” with “Ultra-high purity helium”, “stably pigments-producing mutants” and
“genetic stability”, respectively. Furthermore, we have performed a comprehensive line-by-line
review of the entire manuscript to eliminate awkward phrasing, improve clarity, and ensure the
consistent use of scientific terminology.
Minor Comments 5: Figure legends and tables should include statistical tests and sample sizes (n),
especially for yield comparisons. For instance, in Fig. 2f/g and Fig. 5c.
Thanks for your advice.
In Fig. 2f, the term “genetic frequency” was used to represent the hereditary stability of positive
clones. Thirty-two positive clones were randomly selected from each irradiation treatment for
analysis. This metric reflects the proportion of pigmented clones within each subculture generation
relative to the total number of clones. Error bars are not applicable for this representation.
Fig. 2g compared the average yields of ACT and RED produced by the mutants generated via
UV, ARTP and HEPE irradiation. This figure legend has been revised to include statistical tests and
sample sizes. The detailed information were as follows: Data are presented as mean ± SEM from
three independent samples, each performed with three replicates (n = 3). Significance was assessed
by one-way ANOVA. *, P < 0.05; **, P < 0.01; ***, P < 0.001.
We have also added appropriate statistical tests and sample sizes descriptions to Fig. 5c. The
detailed information was as follows: Data are presented as mean ± SEM from three independent
experiments (n = 3). Significance was assessed by one-way ANOVA. *, P < 0.05; ***, P < 0.001.
Minor Comments 6: In the discussion, it would be helpful to comment briefly on the regulatory or
biosafety implications of using HEPE-induced strains for industrial-scale production, especially
when compared to genome-edited strains.
Beyond laboratory efficacy, the industrial-scale application of HEPE-mutagenized strains
warrants consideration of regulatory and biosafety. Unlike genome editing, which often falls under
genetically modified organism regulations due to the use of foreign DNA or targeted genetic
modifications, HEPE is a non-transgenic method that avoids exogenous DNA integration. However,
the extensive and random mutations induced by HEPE demand rigorous stability and safety
assessments to ensure consistent industrial performance. The substantial genomic alterations still
require thorough evaluation to guarantee product safety and environmental safety before large-scale
use. We have now added some description in the Discussion section (lines 351-358) that address
this point.
Minor Comments 7: In the Hi-C analysis, the manuscript claims HEPE-induced SVs are
“uniformly distributed”, but does not quantify the degree of randomness or clustering. Consider
including an enrichment or dispersion analysis to support this observation.
Thanks for your advice.
According to your suggestion, we have incorporated a dispersion analysis utilizing genome
binning to characterize the distribution of HEPE-induced SVs. Based on the SVs data, a 10-kb
sliding window approach was employed to assess the dispersion of SVs across the genome. Using
the SVs count distribution obtained from the sliding-window analysis, we further calculated the
coefficient of variation (CV) and performed a chi-square goodness-of-fit test to evaluate whether
the SVs distribution in each group significantly deviated from a uniform pattern. The CV serves as
a measure of dispersion: a lower value indicates a more uniform distribution, while a higher value
reflects greater variability and clustering. The results demonstrated that HEPE group had a more
uniform genomic distribution of SVs than the UV and ARTP groups, as evidenced by its lower CV
value, although all groups significantly deviated from a uniform distribution (Table S3). In light of
this result, we have updated the text describing the distribution of SVs induced by UV, ARTP or
HEPE in the Result section (lines 155-159).

While the high-yielding phenotype of these metabolites demonstrated hereditary stability in

current limitations in time and resources, such experiments have not been incorporated into the
present study. We plan to conduct these investigations in collaboration with industrial partners in

but no direct comparison reference values were given. Please provide comparative data of existing

We have now provided direct comparisons with the current production records for both

In our current study, we did not directly design experiments to specifically measure plasmid
stability or chromosomal integration post-HEPE exposure. However, wo can provide the following
observations based on our existing data. As HEPE introduces random mutations throughout the
entire genome, plasmids within engineered strains could potentially be damaged following HEPE
exposure. However, in clones selected based on improved production of the target metabolite after
HEPE treatment, the plasmids they harbored remained stable and continued to express the target
metabolite efficiently. The fact that we successfully obtained high-producing mutants from
engineered E. coli strains (which contained plasmid-based expression system for mccJ25) suggests
that the core engineered constructs remained functional after HEPE treatment. Moreover, the yield
of mccJ25 remained stable during the ten consecutive subcultures in the HEPE mutagenized mutants,
indirectly indicates that the essential genetic elements were not universally disrupted by the

Reviewer 3:
Major Comments 1: While this advancement is impressive, the manuscript lacks many details,
making it difficult to read and interpret. For example, the authors conclude that double-strand breaks
are the ideal marker of genetic rearrangements conducive to producing secondary metabolites, but
this has not been systematically studied. The authors should either conduct additional work to
demonstrate that double-strand breaks are the critical markers of strain improvement or tone down
this claim throughout the manuscript.
Thanks for your advice.
DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) catalyze structure variation formation10, which drive
microbial evolution by altering genomic architecture, transcriptional networks, and metabolic
output7-9. Based on the "DSB–SV–phenotype" theoretical framework, we hypothesized that a
mutagenic method capable of inducing more DSBs would likely generate more SVs, thereby more
effectively activating silent metabolic pathways. To test this hypothesis, we systematically
compared three physical mutagenesis methods-UV, ARTP, and HEPE-in terms of DSB levels,
secondary metabolite activation efficiency, and genomic variation profiles in Streptomyces lividans
1326. Both TUNEL assay and plasmid linearization experiments showed that HEPE treatment
produced more DSBs compared to UV and ARTP (Fig.1, Fig. S1). Phenotypic results revealed that
HEPE demonstrated higher activation efficiency for the actinorhodin (ACT) and undecylprodigiosin
(RED) gene clusters than UV and ARTP (Fig.2). The sequencing results indicated that three
treatments did not differ significantly in the number of indels or SNVs. The key difference lay in
the fact that HEPE induced more SVs (Fig. 3a). Additionally, we supplemented two critical
experiments: transcriptome sequencing (RNA-seq) and comparative 3D genome conformation
analysis between S. lividans 1326 WT and mutant strains. The results revealed that the mutant
displayed extensive transcriptional reprogramming (Figure S4) and a globally altered 3D
chromosome architecture (Figure 3c-d). This global change is unlikely to be caused by small-scale
SNVs or indels, but is primarily attributed to large-scale SVs.
Based on these results, we thought more double-strand breaks means the formation of more
structure variations, which disrupt both the linear DNA sequence and the higher-order 3D
conformation, thereby driving the observed enhancement in metabolite production. Nevertheless,
these findings remain insufficient to establish DSB as a generalizable marker for predicting the
metabolic activation potential of microbial strains. In accordance with your recommendation, we
have tone down this claim in this manuscript. We will conduct additional experiments to
demonstrate the link between the DSBs and the strain improvement in our future work.
Major Comments 2: The general applicability of the method is also questionable. HEPE requires
unique instrumentation that is not widely accessible. The authors should be aware of this limitation.
As you rightly noted, the requirement for specialized accelerators represents the limitation of
HEPE application. However, such equipment is commonly available in research institutions.
Moreover, its operation is highly efficient: samples are transported via a conveyor belt to the
irradiation source, allowing for the simultaneous processing of numerous samples in a rapid manner.
Therefore, through collaboration with relevant research facilities to access this instrumentation, the
method remains feasible for practical research applications. We have explicitly acknowledged this
constraint in the revised manuscript (line 334) and expanded our discussion regarding both the
advantages and limitations of HEPE in lines 335-350.
Minor Comments 1: Line 121 states that the ACT and RED biosynthetic gene clusters are cryptic,
but this is not well established. After fermentation on various media, Streptomyces lividans is known
to be a prolific producer of both pigments. Therefore, the authors should be cautious with such
definitive statements. It might be that these pigments are produced more rapidly in mutant than in
wild-type strains, but claiming that the BGCs are cryptic contradicts decades of Streptomyces
research. Additionally, it's unclear whether the authors have quantified the increase in pigment
production beyond the simple observation of red and blue colonies. This lack of detail is a recurring
issue throughout the manuscript.
As you stated, the ACT and RED biosynthetic gene clusters are activated after fermentation on
various media. We have corrected the statement in the main text as follows: These two BGCs are
lowly expressed or cryptic under certain culture conditions, and exhibits blue and red colors upon
their activations (in lines 122-123). Additionally, we have quantified the increase in pigment
production beyond the simple observation of red and blue colonies. Three mutants from each
irradiation method were selected to evaluate the pigment production stabilities and enhancement.
The production of ACT and RED were determined by the absorbance at 600 nm and 530 nm,
respectively. The specific details were described in lines 473-480, and the results were showed in
the Fig.2g.

with three replicates (n = 3). Significance was assessed by one-way ANOVA. *, P < 0.05; **, P <

Minor Comments 2: Line 129, the authors report mutation rates in percentage, but referring to
such values as rates, which are defined as a measure of change over time, is confusing and perhaps

The values we reported (as percentages) represent the proportion or frequency of observed
mutations in our cell population at a specific time point, rather than a rate measured over time.
Accordingly, we have replaced 'mutation rate' with the more accurate term 'mutation frequency'

We apologize for omitting the scale bars in the panels of Figure 1. We have added them to the
panels.

difficult to read. For example:
Line 51, “which are normally inefficient to achievable secondary metabolites…” is grammatically
incorrect
Line 54 “this challenge causes the slow pace of drug discovery...” The use of the word ‘cause’ here
is questionable. A word like contributes is probably better.

We have corrected these grammatical errors you mentioned above. Moreover, we have
carefully reviewed the entire manuscript and corrected some perplexing sentence structures.
Finally, we would like to once again express our sincere gratitude to the three reviewers for
their constructive comments on our manuscript, as well as thank the editor for the additional time
granted to complete the revision and for supporting us in performing additional experiments.
We hope that our response satisfactorily addresses the key points. And again, we are sincerely
grateful to all the reviewers for their positive assessment of our work and their insightful suggestions.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors show that HEPE generates thousands of structural variants per genome, yet the RNA-
seq analysis is restricted to the focus of two best-characterized clusters (ACT and RED).
Streptomyces typically harbours 20–30 biosynthetic gene clusters per strain, so the central question
is: how many of these remaining BGCs are also transcriptionally perturbed, and why do only a
minority produce detectable metabolites? A simple differential-expression count across all
annotated BGCs should be provided, together with the percentage of clusters whose key
biosynthetic genes move from silent to expressed after HEPE treatment. If the majority remain silent
despite massive structural change, the authors should discuss the buffering mechanisms that allow
the cell to tolerate wholesale genomic rearrangements without global metabolic chaos—an issue
highly relevant to microbial robustness and genome evolution. I therefore recommend:
1. Re-analyse the existing RNA-seq data set to quantify expression changes in every annotated BGC,
and present the data as a new supplementary figure.
Thanks for your advice.
In the present study, transcriptome sequencing was performed on the S. lividans 1326 wild-
type strain and its three mutants generated via HEPE treatment. Bioinformatic analysis using
AntiSMASH tool identified 27 putative BGCs within the S. lividans 1326 genome. As suggested,
we conducted differential expression analysis for all 27 annotated BGCs. The results are
summarized in a new figure and table (Figure S5，Table S5).
Figure S5a-c indicate that HEPE treatment induced widespread transcriptional perturbations in
most BGCs. At the cluster level, a general spatial pattern can be observed: BGCs located near the
both ends of the chromosome tended to be downregulated, while those in the central region were
generally upregulated. This may be related to an overall loosening of chromosomal architecture in
the HEPE-treated mutants. Quantitatively, approximately one-third (9 BGCs) were down-regulated
and 41% (11 BGCs) were up-regulated.
A more detailed gene-level analysis is provided in Figure S5d and Table S5. At this level, the
proportions of differentially expressed genes varied among the three mutant strains, consistent with
the stochastic nature of HEPE mutagenesis. Among differentially expressed genes, 5-13% were up-
regulated, with key biosynthetic genes representing only 1.6-6.5% of the total in these mutants.
Furthermore, within a gene cluster, transcriptional changes among key genes or between key genes
and regulators may be inconsistent, preventing the coordinated activation of the entire metabolic
pathway. This limited and stochastic up-regulation of critical pathway components appears
insufficient to drive the coordinated expression required for efficient metabolites biosynthesis and
accumulation, likely explaining why only a minority of corresponding metabolites were detected.

2. Add a dedicated Discussion section that addresses why extensive SV load does not translate into
widespread metabolite diversification: possible explanations include redundancy of pathway-
specific regulators, dosage sensitivity of metabolic precursors, or rapid compensatory mutations that
silence newly formed clusters.
Thank you for suggesting possible explanations for this issue. We have added a dedicated
Discussion section that addresses why extensive SV load does not translate into widespread
metabolite diversification. The specific content is as follows and has been incorporated into the
manuscript at lines 348-359.
Despite a high load of SVs constantly reshaping the genomic landscape of BGCs, the observed
chemical diversity may represent only a fraction of their genomic potential. This discrepancy arises
from multi-layered biological constraints. Many secondary metabolite BGCs are governed by
dedicated pathway-specific regulators, yet such regulatory networks frequently exhibit functional
redundancy or hierarchical control55. Consequently, even if genomic rearrangements activate silent
BGCs, their expression may still be repressed by upstream global regulators or remain inactive due
to the absence or dysfunction of required pathway-specific activators. Furthermore, secondary
metabolites biosynthesis depends critically on precursor molecules supplied by primary metabolism.
Newly activated BGCs often impose a metabolic burden, leading to insufficient precursor flux and
ultimately aborted product synthesis. Under evolutionary pressure, activated gene clusters may
undergo secondary mutations that rapidly silence these resource-consuming BGCs to restore growth
fitness. This silencing-driven selection further explains why novel compounds frequently escape
detection at the final stage of analyses.
3. Relate these findings to the broader literature on genome instability and stress resistance in
filamentous actinobacteria, highlighting how Streptomyces can apparently “absorb” large-scale
chromosomal restructuring while maintaining viability.
We have followed your guidance to review the relevant literature and have now integrated the
findings of this study. A corresponding discussion has been added at lines 309-324 of the revised
manuscript. The specific content is presented below.
HEPE irradiation can induce extensive SVs in the Streptomyces genome while preserving
cellular viability. This resilience can be attributed to its inherent genomic instability and stress
response strategies. The Streptomyces genome appears architecturally organized to tolerate
restructuring. Essential genes for primary metabolism and growth are clustered in the core region
of the chromosome, while secondary metabolite BGCs and other adaptive features are often located
on more plastic chromosomal arms. This compartmentalization allows the arms to undergo HEPE-
induced SVs while buffering the essential core from fatal disruption. Furthermore, Streptomyces
possesses linear chromosomes with terminal inverted repeats (TIRs), creating "open ends" that
facilitate end-joining recombination and chromosomal rearrangements46. Such genomic instability
drives Streptomyces’ rapid evolution, aiding adaptation to competitive soil microenvironments.
Under stresses like HEPE irradiation, genomic instability increases, triggering an SOS-like response.
Streptomyces also harbors diverse two-component systems and mobile genetic elements that
mediate DNA recombination and repair upon sensing stress signals46, 47. Robust DNA repair systems
allow it to withstand radiation-induced DNA damage and even convert such damage into genetic
diversity. This genomic instability coupled with robust stress resistance enables Streptomyces not
only to survive tenaciously but also to evolve into a vast natural repository of medicinal compounds.
4. The authors need to deposit the raw FASTQ files of the RNA-seq data and the processed count
matrix in a public database (e.g., NCBI GEO or ENA) and include the accession code in the Data
Availability section prior to acceptance.
The raw RNA-seq FASTQ files and the processed gene count matrix generated in this study
have been deposited in the NCBI GEO database under accession number GSE315268 (publicly
accessible). This accession code has been included in the Data Availability section (lines 780-782).

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Small-molecule metabolites are key pharmaceutical resources embedded in complex organismal metabolomes. Scalable microbial production depends on metabolic activation capacity, which in turn requires efficient genetic variation. Structural variants (SVs), key drivers of phenotypic diversity, are pivotal for organism evolution, yet their highly efficient induction remains challenging. While DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) facilitate SVs formation, existing mutagenesis technologies struggle to balance high DSB efficiency with cellular preservation, particularly in microbial strain improvement for metabolite production. Conventional irradiation methods suffer from low SVs induction rates, making strain enhancement a lengthy and labor-intensive process. Here, we systematically compare six irradiation technologies in Streptomyces lividans 1326 and identify high-energy pulsed electron beams (HEPE) as an approach which effectively induces strong DSBs while preserving cellular integrity. This results in extensive SVs that reshape genome sequences and 3D chromatin structure, leading to activation of secondary metabolite production. By integrating HEPE with high-throughput metabolomics (HEPE-HiTMS), we discover two secondary metabolites with unusual C-N linkage, respectively. Applied across various microorganisms, HEPE enables record-high clavulanic acid and microcin J25 production, and markedly increases lovastatin yields. With its ability to induce SVs with minimal cytotoxicity, HEPE represents a powerful tool for cryptic metabolite discovery and industrial strain development.

---

## Introduction

Microbial metabolites have profoundly influenced human civilization-from traditional brewing and vinegar making to the discovery of antibiotics-and remain central to industries such as pharmaceuticals, energy and agriculture1. However, under natural conditions, the biosynthesis of metabolites is tightly regulated, with over 80% being produced at limited production levels or even undetectable2. These insufficiently produced metabolites, especially the fully silent secondary metabolites (SMs), are normally difficult to access through cultivation optimization or simple regulatory engineering, and require extensive and profound genetic rewiring to activate. This challenge contributes to the slow pace of drug discovery and extended timelines in industrial strain development. At the core lies a major bottleneck: the lack of efficient, scalable tools to boost metabolic output3.

Gene mutations, particularly structural variations (SVs > 50 bp)4–6, drive microbial evolution by disproportionately altering genomic architecture, transcriptional networks, and metabolic output7–9. While DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) catalyze SV formation10,11, spontaneous DSBs in microbes under natural conditions are extremely rare. This limits natural mutation rates and hampers the efficiency of strain improvement for metabolites production12–14. Irradiation mutagenesis accelerates evolution by introducing severe DNA damage, thereby inducing intense mutation15. Traditional approaches such as UV and γ-ray irradiation, as well as newer methods like atmospheric room-temperature plasma (ARTP), have long been used in microbial mutagenesis16. However, these techniques are rarely used for activating cryptic metabolites, and they fail to achieve both robust DSB induction and high cellular integrity, which are essential for maximizing SV formation and mutant survival17.

To address this challenge, we systematically compare six different types of irradiation technologies using the model host Streptomyces lividans 1326 (S. lividans 1326): UV and microwave (MW; low-energy non-ionizing radiation)18; X-ray and γ-ray (high-energy ionizing radiation)19; ARTP20 and HEPE (particle radiation)21. We evaluate their capacity to induce DSBs, preserve cellular integrity, and enhance the production of SMs with diverse expression levels22. Among them, HEPE, previously unreported in microbial mutagenesis, emerges as superior, generating intense SVs that remodel genome sequences and 3D chromatin architecture, significantly boosting metabolic capacity. By coupling HEPE with high-throughput metabolomics (HEPE-HiTMS), we rapidly identify and characterize two structurally novel, previously undetectable compounds—griseobrucins and fradibactin with rare C-N linkage, respectively. Extending HEPE to diverse microorganisms (actinobacteria, bacteria, fungi), we achieve yield enhancements in the production of clavulanic acid23 (2×; record-level), lovastatin24 (7.3×), and antimicrobial peptide microcin J2525 (3×; highest reported). Our findings establish HEPE as a transformative mutagenesis tool that enhances metabolic output by driving SV-based genomic remodeling with minimal cytotoxicity. This approach provides a powerful tool for the discovery of bioactive compounds and applications in industrial biotechnology.

---

## Results

DNA damage induction and cellular integrity across six irradiation technologies
To evaluate and compare the DNA double-strand break (DSB) induction efficiency of six irradiation technologies, we performed TdT-mediated dUTP nick end labeling (TUNEL) assays and plasmid linearization analyses. Given the heterogeneity in irradiation types and energy levels among the six technologies, direct comparison of their DNA-damaging effects using identical radiation doses was precluded. We thus irradiated samples with four escalating dose levels, covering the commonly used upper and lower detection limits of irradiation instruments to enable cross-platform analysis21 (see Materials and Methods).

Mycelia of S. lividans 1326 were irradiated with UV, MW, X-rays, γ-rays, ARTP, and HEPE, after which the cells were harvested and subjected to TUNEL assays to detect single- and double-strand DNA breaks (SSBs and DSBs). Results from fluorescence microscopy clearly revealed no detectable signals in UV-, MW-, or ARTP-treated samples at their respective maximum irradiation durations of 600s, 180s and 300s. Samples treated with X-ray and γ-ray exhibited faint signals at low doses but pronounced fluorescence at the highest doses of 100 Gy and 3 kGy respectively. Whereas HEPE generated strong signals even at minimal doses of 1 kGy, with intensity increasing in a dose-dependent manner (Fig. 1a). These findings indicate that X-ray, γ-ray, and HEPE possess robust penetration capacity to induce intracellular DNA damage, with HEPE causing the most severe DNA damage, followed by γ-ray and X-ray. In contrast, UV, MW, and ARTP showed limited penetration capacity for DNA breaks.

To further investigate DSB induction by each method, plasmid pIJ773 (4.3 kb) was irradiated and then analyzed by plasmid linearization assay. Supercoiled-to-linear conformational shifts, indicative of extracellular DSBs, were negligible in UV- and MW-treated samples even at their maximum doses. Conversely, HEPE, γ-ray, ARTP, and X-ray induced progressive plasmid linearization, with efficiency ranked as HEPE > γ-ray > ARTP > X-ray. Notably, HEPE almost fully linearized pIJ773 at minimal doses, indicating its most powerful DSBs induction effect (Supplementary Fig. 1). These results demonstrate that DSB induction correlates with radiation energy levels26, and HEPE, the energy of which can easily reach industrial safety limits (10 MeV)-exhibits unparalleled efficiency in DSB generation.

Next, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of irradiated S. lividans 1326 cells revealed severe lysis and structural damage in UV-, MW-, X-ray-, and γ-ray treated samples at subminimal doses (90s, 60s, 50 Gy, 0.5 kGy), respectively. In contrast, ARTP (90s) and HEPE (6 kGy) caused observable damage at submaximal doses, with negligible effects observed at subminimal doses (Fig. 1b). This highlights the superiority of particle radiation (HEPE, ARTP) in preserving cellular integrity over ionizing and non-ionizing radiation.

Based on these results, HEPE shows the strongest DSB induction for generating SVs while causing minimal cell damage, an optimal balance for enhancing microbial metabolite production. Given its limited application in mutagenesis breeding, we selected two competitive controls for further evaluation: ARTP, which also moderately induces DSBs with minimal cell damage but has limited penetration, and UV, which is the most cost-effective and accessible.

Evaluating metabolite production in S. lividans 1326 by UV, ARTP and HEPE
The general host S. lividans 1326 contains the biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) of pigments ACT (actinorhodin) and RED (undecylprodigiosin). These two BGCs are lowly expressed or cryptic under certain culture conditions, and exhibits blue and red colors upon their activations22. We compared mutagenic efficiencies of HEPE, UV, and ARTP by screening pigmented mutants. S. lividans was irradiated and the resulting positive colorful mutants were screened, counted, and evaluated for phenotypic stability and the production of ACT and RED (Fig. 2a). A total of 308,672 surviving colonies (with and without blue or red color) were counted, ensuring that each irradiation dose contributed over 5000 colonies for subsequent mutagenic efficiency analysis (Fig. 2b). The blue and red pigmented colonies, identified as positive mutants with activated ACT and RED production, were used to calculate the positive mutation frequency. At optimal HEPE dose (6 kGy), the positive mutation frequency reached 10.7%, which is 8.9 and 6.7 times higher than that of UV and ARTP, respectively, despite comparable mortality rates (>97%, Fig. 2c–e).

To further assess the production stability of the mutations induced by the three technologies, totally 96 dual-colored mutants, 32 each from UV, ARTP and HEPE were randomly selected and subcultured for ten generations. The proportion of mutants that retained pigmentation in each generation was calculated (Supplementary Fig. 2). After ten rounds of subculturing, 60.9% of HEPE-induced mutants stably produced ACT/RED, exceeding the rates for UV (29.7%) and ARTP (42.2%), which confirm the superior genetic stability of the HEPE-derived mutants (Fig. 2f). Meanwhile, HEPE mutants exhibited higher average ACT/RED yields. Analysis of ACT/RED production at generations 3, 5, 7 and 10 in three stably pigments-producing mutants from each method showed that HEPE not only outperforms UV and ARTP in mutation efficiency but also in production stability and yield enhancement (Fig. 2g). This suggests that mutations induced by HEPE are less readily repaired than those of UV and ARTP.

Investigation of genomic and 3D chromatin alterations in S. lividans 1326 induced by HEPE
To investigate the mechanism underlying the superior mutagenic efficiency of HEPE irradiation, we sequenced all the genomes of 96 pigmented mutant strains previously obtained through UV, ARTP, and HEPE irradiation. Compared to the original S. lividans strain, the total number of genetic variants in the UV, ARTP, and HEPE groups was 2817, 2523, and 2545, respectively, with SNVs being the predominant variant type (Fig. 3a, Supplementary Table 1). Although HEPE irradiated mutants did not show increase in SNVs and indels compared to UV and ARTP irradiated mutants (Supplementary Table 1-2), they exhibited a marked increase in the SVs (151), surpassing those induced by UV (70) and ARTP (111). This confirmed our expectation that HEPE induces more DSBs, leading to a higher number of SVs10,27,28 (Fig. 3a). Notably, among all SV types, 56 translocations (TRAs) in HEPE mutants exceeded UV/ARTP by nearly 6-fold, indicating frequent occurrence of non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) in the genomes of HEPE mutants28–30 (Fig. 3a).

A comparison of the genomic distributions of SVs induced by UV, ARTP, and HEPE irradiation in S. lividans was performed using a dispersion analysis with genome binning (see Methods). The result revealed that HEPE group had a more uniform genomic distribution of SVs than the UV and ARTP groups, as evidenced by its lower CV value, although all groups significantly deviated from a uniform distribution (Supplementary Table 3). Circos plot visualization further illustrated the SVs distribution patterns (Fig. 3b, Supplementary Table 4). In the UV and ARTP groups, SVs were predominantly located at the arm ends, with TRA occurring between spatially proximate left and right arms. In contrast, the HEPE group exhibited SVs also abundantly in the core regions. Accordingly, TRA events in the HEPE group were observed between arms as well as between arm ends and the core region.

SVs can exert a greater impact on phenotype changes. This impact is not solely attributed to larger alterations in DNA sequence, dramatic changes in the three-dimensional (3D) chromosome conformation could also play a key role compared to SNVs and indels31. To investigate potential alterations in 3D conformation in HEPE mutant, we compared the chromosome architecture of the wild type (WT) and the mutant strain (H_D1) using high-throughput chromosome conformation capture (Hi-C). First, circus plot (Fig. 3c) of the significant interactions (see Methods) revealed a substantial increase in interaction number in mutant (8830) compared to WT (458). Furthermore, the 3D architecture (Fig. 3d) showed that WT maintain a compact chromosome organization, whereas the mutant exhibited a more relaxed conformation. This difference can be elucidated by the differential interaction and compact analysis (see Methods). As shown in the differential interaction heatmap and the compact matrix (Supplementary Fig. 3), WT is enriched in long-range interactions, maintaining its tighter spatial connectivity. In contrast, mutant showed enhanced short-range interactions, corresponding to a looser spatial organization. This result indicated that mutant’s reinforced local interactions disrupt the native compact 3D genome architecture. This structural relaxation likely facilitates the binding of RNA polymerase and other transcriptional machinery to DNA by increasing accessibility to regulatory regions and gene promoters, ultimately modulating the expression of secondary metabolite BGCs32.

Transcriptome sequencing was subsequently performed on the S. lividans 1326 WT strain and HEPE mutants exhibiting activation of the act or red gene cluster. Differential expression analysis confirmed substantial transcriptional alterations, including the significant upregulation of multiple genes within the red or act gene cluster (Supplementary Fig. 4). HEPE treatment also induced widespread transcriptional perturbations across numerous other BGCs (Supplementary Fig. 5, Supplementary Table 5). Additionally, random SVs can have possible unintended effects, such as growth defects. To assess off-target consequences of HEPE mutagenesis, three mutants were selected for phenotype and growth curve analysis. Compared to WT strain, mutants exhibited reduced sporulation and delayed growth (Supplementary Fig. 6). Transcriptome data linked this phenotype to a marked downregulation of the sporulation-associated genes apA and the regulatory factors whiB and whiD, which control cell division and spore septum formation33,34 (Supplementary Table 6).

Collectively, this dual disruption of DNA sequence and 3D chromatin architecture likely drives enhanced metabolite production35,36. These results support our hypothesis that HEPE generates more SVs, which induce more intense dual alterations of DNA sequence and 3D chromosome conformation, thereby leading to the higher production of ACT and RED, as previously reported in S. coelicolor31.

Application of HEPE for cryptic metabolites discovery
Given the demonstrated efficiency of HEPE in inducing extensive genomic alterations, we developed the HEPE-HiTMS workflow, a strategy which couples HEPE irradiation with high-throughput metabolomics to evaluate its potential in activating fully cryptic SMs, potentially uncovering novel structural metabolites. HEPE-HiTMS integrates BGC activation with metabolomic profiling as readout37 (Fig. 4a). Resulting MS data were computationally amalgamated into a 3D plot, correlating metabolite intensity and m/z of the compounds detected across mutants to enable algorithm-driven metabolomes analysis38.

We randomly selected two streptomycetes species, Streptomyces griseobrunneus CGMCC 29023 and Streptomyces fradiae CGMCC 29024. S. griseobrunneus was firstly irradiated with HEPE; approximately 120 mutagenic clones were cultured for MS acquisition using a high-throughput approach. The metabolomes were visualized in a 3D plot, revealing three significantly induced metabolites (m/z 386.1, 404.1, and 418.2) in the 300–500 m/z range, which were absent in the parental strain (Fig. 4b, c, Supplementary Fig. 7). The activated metabolome was further annotated using FUNEL, which confirmed that compound m/z 404.1 appears to be novel, with no matches in NPAtlas or COCONUT database (Supplementary Data 1)39. Scaling fermentation of high-yield mutants enabled purification and structural elucidation of these compounds, designated griseobrucins A-C (1-3).

Analysis of 1D/2D NMR revealed griseobrucin A as a methylated diketopiperazine (DKP) conjugated to histidine via an unusual C-N bond, rather than the canonical amide linkage40, while griseobrucins B and C are hydrolytic derivatives (Fig. 4d, Supplementary Fig. 8–10, Supplementary Table 7–9). X-ray diffraction resolved griseobrucin C’s absolute configuration (CCDC number 2432012), which is retained in variants A and B (Fig. 4d, Supplementary Fig. 11, Supplementary Table 10).

We next applied HEPE-HiTMS pipeline to S. fradiae. About 120 obtained clones were subjected to generate a 3D plot metabolomic profiling, revealing two strongly activated metabolites with identical molecular weight (m/z 890.5), undetectable in the parental strain within the 800–1000 m/z range (Fig. 4e–f, Supplementary Fig. 7). FUNEL analysis confirmed their novelty, with no match in public databases (Supplementary Data 1). These two compounds, named fradibactin A (4) & B, were purified from scaled fermentation for structural characterization.

1D/2D NMR analyses identified fradibactins as two enantiomers of hybrids siderophores merging hydroxamate and carboxylate groups, containing a unique C-N double bond with Z configuration, a linkage unreported in known hydroxamate-type siderophores (Fig. 4g, Supplementary Fig. 12, Supplementary Table 11). This unique structural element prompted us to investigate its BGC. AntiSMASH mining uncovered two hydroxamate-associated BGCs41 (Supplementary Fig. 13). Targeted gene inactivation localized fradibactins biosynthesis to the fdn cluster, which harbors an atypical aminobutyrate-2-oxoglutarate aminotransferase (fdnA) adjacent to conserved hydroxamate formation genes (fdnB-F), implicating fdnA in C-N double bond formation (Supplementary Fig. 14, Supplementary Table 12, 13). The successful discovery of the cryptic griseobrucins and fradibactins demonstrates HEPE’s exceptional capacity to activate metabolites, particularly those fully undetectable metabolites through targeted structural variations, positioning HEPE-HiTMS as a robust platform for discovering cryptic microbial metabolites in the future.

HEPE-induced yield increasing of clavulanic acid in industrial Streptomycete
Having demonstrated HEPE’s effectiveness in activating cryptic metabolites, we next applied it to boost the production of targeted metabolites in industrial strains. Unlike wild-type strains, these industrial strains had already undergone conventional mutagenesis and extensive screening, resulting in optimized metabolite production. Our objective was to leverage HEPE mutagenesis to achieve further yield improvement that are unattainable through conventional methods. We firstly selected Streptomyces clavuligerus 70116-an industrial clavulanic acid overproducer derived from WT S. clavuligerus 3585 through 6 years of conventional mutagenesis (non-HEPE) and strain selection (Fig. 5a). Approximately 104-105 spores of S. clavuligerus were subjected to HEPE irradiation on ISP2 agar plates following S. lividans mutagenesis protocol. A total of 110 surviving colonies were selected and fermented in an optimized medium. Comparison of clavulanic acid yields revealed that 27 out of 110 mutant clones exhibited at least a 10% increase in titer (Fig. 5b). The high mutation rate indicates that HEPE mutagenesis is not compromised by prior conventional mutations.

The highest-yielding mutant H_M32 reached a clavulanic acid titer of 5.5 g/L in flasks after 6 d fermentation, representing a 60% increase over the original strain (3.5 g/L). After confirming its productions stability over five rounds of subculturing (Supplementary Fig. 15a), H_M32 was advanced to large-scale cultures. It reached a yield of 6.3 g/L in a 5 L benchtop bioreactor, which signifies an additional 15% increase over the starting strain and is comparable to the record-high of 6.11 g/L23 (Fig. 5c).

To investigate the mechanism underlying the progressive increase in clavulanic acid production among these producers, we performed whole-genome sequencing on the WT, the starting strain 70116, and the highest-yielding mutant H_M32. Analysis of genome variations revealed that strain 70116, which underwent 5 rounds of mixed mutagenesis from WT (Fig. 5c), accumulated a large number of variations compared to the wild type, including 265 SNVs, 29 indels, and 7 SVs, collectively resulting in the 2.3 g/L increase in clavulanic acid production compared to WT strain. In contrast, the HEPE-irradiated mutant H_M32 achieves 2.8 g/L over 70116 with fewer total mutations (36 SNVs, 16 indels, 5 SVs) but a significantly higher proportion of SVs (Fig. 5c). This result underscores that SV frequency, rather than the total mutation count is the key driver of phenotypic enhancement, aligning with SVs’ powerful impact on transcriptional regulation and 3D genome architecture.

Application of HEPE for enhancing metabolites production in diverse industrial species
With the success in streptomyces, we extended the application of HEPE to diverse microbial taxa to evaluate its broad mutagenic potential across other bacteria and fungi. For comparative purpose, UV and ARTP were included alongside HEPE. Moreover, to apply HEPE to plasmid-dependent heterologous expression, which requires unstable multicopy plasmids and can compromise long-term strain performance, we selected an engineered Escherichia coli CGMCC 16349 strain designed for heterologous production of the antimicrobial peptide microcin J25 (mccJ25)42. Following UV, ARTP, and HEPE irradiation, 16.3% of HEPE-treated mutants exhibited >2-fold increase in mccJ25 yield, outperforming UV and ARTP (Fig. 6a–d). Notably, the top 3 mutants resulted in >3-fold yield enhancements, and remained stable after 10 rounds of subculturing in 100 mL flasks (Supplementary Fig. 15b). In scale-up 40 L bioreactors, the best mutant produced mccJ25 at a titer of 7.5 g/L, surpassing the previous literature yield of 4 g/L25 (Fig. 6e, f).

Next, we evaluated HEPE, UV, and ARTP irradiation in filamentous fungi, which are prolific producers of pharmaceutically relevant metabolites43. We selected the lovastatin-producing strain Monascus purpureus MY2, which was generated by 3 rounds of irradiation on a WT strain Y2, for this study24. Each irradiation treatment gave 60 surviving colonies for solid-phase fermentation and lovastatin analysis. HEPE irradiation (2 kGy) generated 13.3% mutants with over 2-fold yield increases, far exceeding UV and ARTP (Fig. 6g–j). Only 48.3% of HEPE mutant exhibited reduced production, compared to 68.3% (UV) and 75.0% (ARTP). The top-performing HEPE mutant was subcultured for five generations in 1 L solid-phase fermentation system to assess lovastatin production stability. The results indicated that lovastatin yield remained generally consistent across generations (Supplementary Fig. 15c). Furthermore, this mutant exhibited a more than 6-fold yield enhancement in 4 L solid-phase fermentation container, reaching a titer of 29 mg/g-nearing industrial benchmarks (Fig. 6k).

Collectively, the markedly yield improvements of clavulanic acid, mccJ25, and lovastatin across actinobacteria, proteobacteria, and fungi underscore the remarkable superiority of HEPE irradiation over UV and ARTP, positioning it as a broadly applicable tool for industrial metabolite enhancement.
